「索爾納」一詞很可能借自與盧維亞語「zurni」（角）、梵文「ṡṛṅga」（角）: The word "sorna" is most likely borrowed from an unknown Indo-European root related to Luvian "zurni" (horn), Sanskrit "ṡṛṅga" (horn), Latin "cornū" and English "horn", and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European "*ḱerh₂-". Folk etymology holds that sorna comes from Persian "sūrnāy" (literally "strong flute"), a compound of "sūr-" (strong) and "-nāy" (flute). Another folk etymology takes the first element from Persian and New Persian "sūr-", meaning "banquet, dining and feasting", hence "banquet flute". As a cognate of "horn", sorna can be translated literally as "horn", a result of the centum–satem division and of Grimm's law later on. Persian also has another wind instrument named "Karnā(y)", whose name appears to be a cognate of "sorna" and "horn", possibly a reborrowing from another language. The modern sorna is still found in places such as Hamadan in Iran.
傳統嗩吶以蘆葦哨片振動發聲，經圓錐木管與銅碗擴音，音色明亮、音量大且高亢，具穿透: The traditional suona sounds through a vibrating reed of cane, amplified by a conical wooden tube and a brass bell: the timbre is bright, the volume large and high, and the sound carries. The player controls the reed with the mouth, adjusting volume, pitch and timbre and making slides, and adjusts the reed as the music requires. The working range in traditional use is about a seventeenth; the most common, high-pitched suona can be blown from its low register up to its high, the very top notes being rarely used. The improved keyed version adds semitone holes and keys, has a range of about a seventeenth plus a semitone, can play semitones and equal temperament, and sounds closer to the oboe while keeping a larger volume and a more direct, carrying quality.
傳統嗩吶的管身以木製成，呈圓錐形；上端裝有木管，並接以蘆葦製哨片，屬雙簧發聲。哨: The body of the traditional suona is made of wood and is conical; a wooden pipe is fitted at the top, with a cane reed attached to it, and the sound is made by a double reed. Once the breath sets the reed vibrating, the sound spreads through the body and out of the brass bell at the lower end. Some sources also record that the mouthpipe joint is metal, commonly brass or copper, and that the bell can be taken off. As for the exact materials of the other parts, the sources do not say.
其形制源於古代伊朗，稱蘇爾奈（Sorna）；另有傳自中亞、阿拉伯或印度之說。約三: The instrument's form comes from ancient Iran, where it is called the sorna; other accounts have it coming from Central Asia, the Arab world or India. It appears in China around the third century, its body developing from solid wood into a wooden pipe with a metal mouthpipe and bell. Ming-dynasty documents establish it in the north, and in the Ming and Qing it was mostly used for weddings and funerals, festivals and military music. It later spread to India, Turkey, the Balkans, Cuba and elsewhere; related instruments include the Korean taepyeongso and the Japanese charumera. From the mid-twentieth century China developed keyed alto, tenor and bass suonas tuned to equal temperament, to fill the middle and low registers of the national orchestra.

In its traditional form a cane reed sits at the top of a wooden pipe and a brass bell at the bottom; you blow with the reed in your mouth, the reed vibrates, and the body and the bell amplify the sound. To hold the instrument, the index, middle, ring and little fingers of the right hand and the thumb, index, middle and ring fingers of the left hand cover the holes. Beginners first practise holding the reed steadily and blowing, then shape the reed with the mouth to change volume, pitch and timbre, and practise slides. The player has to adjust the reed to suit the music.
嗩吶常見於中國傳統吹打樂與鼓吹樂，在婚禮、喪禮、廟會、節慶、軍禮與道教儀式中領奏: The suona is common in the Chinese wind-and-percussion (chuida) and guchui ensembles, leading the music at weddings, funerals, temple fairs, festivals, military ceremonies and Taoist rites, and it also accompanies opera, folk song and dance. The woodwind section of the modern Chinese orchestra uses keyed alto, tenor and bass suonas; in folk settings the traditional form is still the norm. You can hear it in Ren Tongxiang's arrangement of "A Hundred Birds Paying Homage to the Phoenix", in the modernised suona of Cui Jian's song "Nothing to My Name", in the carnival music of Santiago de Cuba and in jazz playing, and in popular performance in Egypt, Turkey, India and elsewhere.

索爾納嗩吶主要採用木質材料製作，管身通常選用杏木或李樹等硬木，具有良好的音質共鳴: The sorna suona is mainly made of wood, the body usually a hardwood such as apricot or plum, which gives good resonance. The double reed is made of cane or buckwheat stalk, carefully shaved and adjusted for the best vibration. The top of the instrument carries a metal reed holder and a bell-shaped opening, and some finer instruments are edged in brass or silver. Bone or ivory may be inlaid around the fingerholes for decoration and protection, and a leather hand strap below them helps the player hold and control the instrument.
索爾納嗩吶音色高亢明亮，穿透力強，具有獨特的鼻音質感。其音域偏高，音色帶有輕微的: The sorna suona is high, bright and strongly carrying, with a distinctive nasal quality. Its range sits high, and the slight nasal resonance makes the sound at once clear and warm, with something of the human voice. The instrument makes its sound through the vibration of a double reed, and in Middle Eastern and Persian music it cuts clearly through the thick texture of drums and strings. Where the Western flute is pure and light, the sorna suona is denser and deeper; beside the Chinese suona its tone is a little softer and more flowing. The resonance comes mainly from the wooden body and the layout of the fingerholes, which lets it produce both a sharp high register and a warm, full middle. Its sound has a strong national character and plenty of expressive power.
